1:
Cyril takes the miracles as credentials: men appointed to holy teaching should be able to work them and be believed ministers of God by those very acts — and in giving power over all devils Christ brought down the pride of the one who had said there is none who shall open his mouth against me. Henry reads the sending as a solution to a limit, Christ being able to be in only one place at a time; he takes the power over all devils as a design of total ruin against the kingdom of darkness, and notes that the healing would make the twelve welcome wherever they came, convincing judgements and gaining affections at once. Clarke presses the pairing into an argument: Luke names both demons and diseases, so either he was mistaken or the two are not the same thing, and the treatments differ — demons cast out, diseases healed. Robertson quietly undercuts that on the next verse: the double office is herald and healer, but Luke uses one verb for healing here and another a line earlier, apparently interchangeably. Gill takes the kingdom preached to be at once the kingdom of grace in men's hearts and the kingdom of glory they are made meet for.

Chrysostom gives three reasons for the stripped equipment — it rendered the disciples unsuspected, held them clear of all care so that they might give their whole study to the word, and taught them their own proper virtue — then raises the objection himself, why no scrip and no second coat and no staff, and answers that Christ meant to rouse them to diligence by taking them from the cares of life. Lightfoot alone notices a difficulty of season: by his reckoning winter was coming on, so forbidding the double garment seems hard, and softens it with rabbinic parallel: a severity by which some clothed themselves in one garment only, R. Jose on righteous men dying of the disease in their bowels from such austerity, and the priests who walked barefoot on the pavement clad in a single garment. Ellicott adds that the better manuscripts give a staff in the singular, the plural probably adopted to harmonise the verse with the other Gospels. Tertullian turns the passage against Marcion: who but the God who feeds the ravens and clothes the flowers would command men to take nothing, and who but the one who forbade muzzling the treading ox? Henry, taking the rule as dependence on Providence, concedes that Paul saw cause not to follow it, labouring with his hands rather than be burdensome.

On the dust shaken off, Ellicott prefers a testimony unto them rather than against them; Robertson notes that Luke's preposition is not the plain dative Mark uses but comes to the same idea; Tertullian will not have it softened, arguing that nobody bears witness except where a case is decided by process, so one who orders conduct submitted to testimony is threatening as a judge. Henry agrees, taking the gesture as binding them over to God's judgement, leaving their blood on their own heads. Then Herod, and Chrysostom marks the delay — it was long before he took notice at all, which shows the pride of a tyrant. Clarke unpacks the verb for his perplexity as a traveller's word, a man at a meeting of roads only one of which leads where he means to go, and adds that a guilty conscience is a continual pest, Herod having murdered John and fearing he should rise and bring his deeds to light. Robertson finds the verb only in Luke's writings and observes that the three rumours are all in the aorist, not the pluperfect the English gives them. Lightfoot explains the third rumour: no prophet but Elias was expected before the Messiah, yet the notion that some ancient prophet should rise was common enough in ordinary talk.
10:
Augustine begins with a question of arrangement rather than meaning: Matthew and Mark take the occasion here to relate how John was killed, but Luke had given that account long before, so after Herod's perplexity he can go straight to the apostles' return. Isidore Peleus reads the withdrawal as moral distance, that Christ hates men of blood and those who keep company with them while they do not leave off their crimes, and so departed after the Baptist's murder. Henry attends to the reporting itself, that they told him all they had done as servants sent on an errand should, so that anything done amiss might be mended next time; and he takes the retreat as a principle, since he who appointed the man-servant and the maid-servant to rest would have his own servants rest too, those in the most public stations needing sometimes to go aside both to recruit their bodies and to furnish their minds for further work. Ambrose asks who the heavenly nourishment is given to and answers by exclusion: not to the indolent, nor to men of rank in the synagogue or in high secular office, nor to those in a city, but to those who seek Christ in the desert.

When the crowds break in on that rest, Henry allows that pious zeal may excuse a little rudeness, as it did with Christ, and observes that the place was no desert where Christ was. Clarke counts five effects of grace in the two verses — the people drawn to follow, kindly received, instructed, healed, and fed — and Bede finds in the same list the evidence that their devotion pleased him, since he received the weary, taught the ignorant, cured the sick and filled the hungry. Robertson notices that both verbs are imperfect, so that he kept on speaking and kept on healing; Ellicott adds a distinction the English cannot carry, that the noun for healing is not built on the verb translated healed but is a more technical word, near to our treatment, and used by Luke almost alone. Then the difficulty. Cyril observes that the command to feed them was one the disciples simply could not obey, having five loaves and two fishes between them, and Robertson notes that their reply is a conditional of the ordinary sort with an unusual conjunction, better rendered unless than except, its noun for food meaning something like our word eatables.

Theophylact takes the order to sit down as a lesson in hospitality, that when we entertain anyone we ought to seat him and give him every comfort. Robertson works the arrangement out in detail: Luke, like Matthew, softens Mark's flat five thousand with an about, the word for the companies means a row of people reclining at a meal and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and the fifties are distributed by a preposition used in that sense. Gill notes the change in the disciples, who stopped disputing the case and did as they were told, ranging the crowd in companies on the green grass. On the breaking, Robertson catches a contrast of tenses that carries the miracle: the breaking is a single aorist act and the giving an imperfect, so that Christ broke once and kept on giving; he adds that the article before the five and the two points back to the disciples' own words, and that where English says break off the Greek says break down. Clarke turns the whole sequence into a rule for ministers, who should exhort their people to hear with reverence, take the bread of life themselves before feeding others, lift the soul often to God, divide rightly the word of truth as portions suited to each, and employ the talents of others for what they cannot do alone.
18:
Henry points out that the setting is Luke's own, not found in the other Evangelists, and draws four things from it: that Christ found time to be alone though he had much public work; that when alone he was praying; that his disciples were with him, so that this was a family prayer, householders and parents and masters being bound to pray with those under them; and that he prayed with them before he examined them, so that the prayer might direct and encourage their answer. Robertson agrees the item is Luke's alone and adds the difficulty in it, since the text says he was praying by himself and that the disciples were with him — a contradiction unless the being alone governs the whole, and Westcott and Hort put in the margin a reading which would mean the disciples fell in with him while he prayed. At any rate, he concludes, the praying was apart from them. Cyril reads the retirement as deliberate instruction, Christ ordaining himself an example by an easy method of teaching, since those who rule a people should surpass them in good deeds; and Gill notes that he prayed as man and mediator.

Ellicott pauses before the narrative to notice what Luke has left out — the walking on the water, the four thousand, the woman of Canaan, the leaven of the Pharisees — and declines to explain it confidently, suggesting only that he may simply not have learnt these things in the course of his inquiries, and drawing the inference that he had not seen the other two Gospels in the form we have them. He also thinks Luke's stress on the prayer deliberate, as though what follows were its result. When the opinions are reported, Robertson observes that they run parallel to the rumours that reached Herod earlier in the chapter, and Henry remarks that the people would make him anything but what he was, adding that ministers who conversed more with ordinary people would know better how to fit instruction to them, since the more a physician is with his patient the better he knows what to do. Ambrose gives the opinions their due and then refuses the whole inquiry: to sift them belongs to a different wisdom from his, for if it sufficed Paul to know nothing but Christ crucified, what more can he desire to know than Christ?

On the confession itself Robertson makes the judgement the passage most needs. The emphatic pronoun shows where the weight falls, and what Peter says is not a fresh discovery but the settled conviction of the disciples, held through the defection of the Galilean crowds and the hostility of the Jerusalem authorities; they had not grasped the spiritual conception of the Messiah that Jesus taught, and their view of it was faulty, but they were clear that he was the Messiah, and there was comfort in that for Jesus, because they were loyal. Ellicott notes that the exact phrase is peculiar to Luke and answers to the Lord's Christ in Simeon's song; Clarke reports that the Coptic and later Persic read it as Thou art Christ God; Henry lets the contrast stand plainly, that this is what discipleship is worth, since they knew better than the crowd. The charge of silence follows, and Robertson supplies its reason: the title carried a political meaning among the Jews, so that its use by the disciples would have led to revolution, as had nearly happened after the feeding of the five thousand. Gill observes that Christ approved the confession and pronounced Peter blessed before laying the charge, and that the suffering foretold was to be borne in person and character, in soul and body, at the hands of God and men and devils alike.
23:
Cyril of Alexandria opens with a military figure that governs the whole passage. Mighty generals encourage trained soldiers not only by promising the honours of victory but by telling them the suffering itself brings glory, since no man wins fame in battle without sometimes taking wounds, and the wound bears witness to the courage of his mind. Christ, he says, argues the same way and for a particular reason: he had just told the disciples that he must endure the malice of the Jews, be mocked and spat upon and killed and rise the third day, and he adds this lest they should suppose that he would suffer for the life of the world while they might live quietly and avoid suffering without blame. Basil takes the following clause carefully, that coming after him cannot mean following his body, which is impossible now that he is in heaven, but a due imitation of his life according to each man's capacity; and Bede reads it as bearing the cross already spoken of and then following one who bore his own.

The one word the commentators fight over is daily. Clarke reports it missing from many reputable manuscripts, versions and fathers, and notes that it is absent from both parallels in Matthew and Mark. Robertson keeps it and makes it the point of the verse, observing that it is peculiar to Luke in this incident, and that the tenses divide the labour — the taking up is an aorist and the following a present, so a man takes up his cross and then keeps on following. He adds that the cross was a familiar sight in Palestine and was already rising before Jesus as his destiny, and that each man has his own to meet and bear. Robertson also notices that the address is to all rather than to the disciples only, which he calls characteristic of Luke, and that the sayings which follow are cast in mercantile terms throughout — gain, lose, forfeit, exchange — though the disciples could not yet understand the words as they applied to a death he had only just begun to speak of.

On the loss Clarke insists that the damage meant is spiritual and says why the qualification matters: temporal damage of any kind might be amply compensated by gaining the world, but a hurt to the soul in the smallest degree could not be indemnified by possessing the universe, since earthly goods repair earthly losses and cannot repair a breach in the peace or holiness of the soul. Ellicott separates the two verbs, the first a direct act of self-destruction and the second the forfeiture of something precious rather than outright rejection, which he thinks slightly softens what precedes. Ambrose turns to the promise at the end and reads the not tasting of death strictly: those who can stand where Christ is will not experience even the slightest perception of death, and what is denied here is not the death of the body but of the soul. Ellicott notes that the glory named as Christ's own, alongside the Father's, is peculiar to Luke's report and agrees with words recorded in John. Robertson observes that the double negative and the figure of tasting death are both rabbinical, and adds the sentence the passage earns: like a physician, Christ tasted death that we might see how to die.
28:
Eusebius reads the scene as proof offered to the eye: having told the disciples the mystery of his coming, Christ proceeds from words to works and shows the image of his kingdom. Bede takes the ascent as a lesson in posture, that those who look for the fruit of the resurrection and would see the King in his glory must keep the dwelling place of their hearts on high and be always at prayer. Robertson locates the mountain as probably Hermon, Peter's confession having been made near Caesarea Philippi, and notes that the purpose of the going up, to pray, is Luke's own addition. John Damascene distinguishes the two kinds of praying: a servant prays by lifting his mind to God, but the mind of Christ, being united to God, prayed in order to lead us by the hand up that ascent and to teach that he is not opposed to the Father but reverences him as his beginning. He adds the old image of the hook hidden under the bait, the tyrant who deceived man with the hope of divinity being himself caught by the clothing of humanity; and sums the verse in a phrase, that prayer is the revelation of divine glory.

Two commentators arrive independently at the same explanation of a word Luke does not use. Ellicott observes that the Evangelist with the most classical culture avoids the term the others employ, because metamorphosis carried the associations Ovid's great poem had fastened on it; Robertson says the same and names the same book. Robertson adds that the compound describing the raiment means to flash forth and stands here alone in the New Testament. Ambrose makes the brightness a measure of the beholder: the word is lessened or increased according to your capacity, and unless you climb to a higher wisdom you do not see what glory is in it — the garments of the Word being the discourses of Scripture, so that as the raiment shone, the sense of the divine words grows clear. On the sleeping he is gentler than expected, reasoning that the brightness of the divine nature overwhelms our bodily senses, since an eye cannot hold even the sun's ray, and that perhaps they were weighed down so as to see the sight after rest, a figure of the resurrection. His conclusion is the sharpest sentence in the pericope: no one sees the glory of Christ except he is watching. Theophylact is blunter: Peter was weak and did what is natural to a man.

Lightfoot supplies what a Jewish reader brought to the two figures: a tradition that Moses should come with Elias, another that Moses was raised alongside Samuel by the witch of Endor, and the saying that Moses did not die but went up into the highest to minister before God. Tertullian uses their presence against Marcion by turning the argument inside out. If Christ came to destroy the Law and the Prophets, why exhibit them on the mountain, why in conversation with him, which marks familiarity, and why associated in his glory, which marks respect? This, he says, is how he destroys them — he irradiates them with his glory; and nothing could better befit the Creator's Christ than to be seen with those to whom he had appeared and speaking with those who had spoken of him. On the subject of that conversation Ellicott notes that Luke alone reports it, and that the word for the departure is remarkable both for being uncommon in that sense and for covering resurrection and ascension as well as death. Robertson presses the same word into a figure: Moses had led the exodus out of Egypt, and Jesus was about to accomplish the exodus of God's people into the promised land on high. Barnes hears the allusion too, calling a saint's death a going forth from captivity to the Canaan in the skies.
37:
Bede reads the descent as part of the design, on the principle that certain places accord with certain events: on the mountain Christ prays and is transfigured and opens the secrets of his glory, and coming down to the lower parts he is met by a crowd; above, the voice of the Father is made known, below, the evil spirits are expelled. Robertson draws a small chronological point from a phrase that is Luke's alone — that it happened on the next day shows the transfiguration took place in the night before — and notes that both the verb for coming down and the verb for meeting are, with one exception each, confined to Luke's writings in the New Testament. Ellicott is interested in what is missing, since Luke leaves out the question about the coming of Elijah which the other two Gospels record here; and his explanation is the one he gave earlier in the chapter, that among the Gentiles Luke wrote for there was no expectation of that coming, so neither the impression nor the difficulties it raised needed correcting.

Two voices notice the same tenderness in the reporting. Ellicott observes that Luke alone calls attention to the boy being an only child, as he alone does at Nain, and that the address here is the commoner word for teacher; Robertson adds that Luke has used the same word for an only child twice already, and that the verb the father uses for looking upon his son is one the medical writers employ for examining a patient carefully. Chrysostom is less gentle with the man, holding that his faith was much weakened, as the Gospels show elsewhere in his own words, help thou my unbelief, and if thou canst. Titus Bost asks why the cure was not simply commanded and answers that Christ made the sufferings public on purpose, bringing those weak in faith to the sight of what was before them; so when the devil perceived him and threw the child down and tore him, the order was deliberate, the affliction shown first and the remedy applied after.

Clarke stops on the phrase for the seizure and shows that it is not a Christian coinage but the ordinary language of pagan writers for supernatural influence. He quotes Herodotus on Scyles, the Scythian king who preferred Greek ways and wished to be initiated privately into the Bacchic mysteries: a Borysthenian slipped out during the ceremony and told the Scythian army that they mocked the Greeks for celebrating the Bacchanals and for saying the god possesses us, and yet the same power had now taken possession of their own king, who was celebrating them and was filled with fury by the god. Clarke's point is that the historian uses the very verb Luke uses, that a demon is the agent in both accounts, and that both writers prove the possession real by its effects — the king raging, and the boy here crying out, convulsed and foaming. He concludes that this was a real possession of the kind that often occurred among worshippers of demons. Robertson, working the same verse, notes only that the adverb for the suddenness is one the medical writers use of the abrupt onset of diseases such as epilepsy.
43:
Ellicott stops on the word for what the crowd wondered at, which is unusual, appears again in the second epistle of Peter in close connection with the transfiguration, and is elsewhere rendered majesty and magnificence — greatness, he suggests, would be the best equivalent here, Luke describing the emotion easterners feel when they say that God is great. He then registers a complaint about the printers: the division of verses at this point is singularly unfortunate, and the new paragraph should begin at the words about their wondering. Cyril makes the same division from the other side and explains why it matters. Everything Jesus did claimed the admiration of all, but what follows is addressed not to all but to the disciples; he had shown his glory on the mountain and had just delivered a man from an evil spirit, and now the passion had to be faced, so that his disciples might well have been perplexed and asked whether they had been deceived in thinking him God. That is why they are told to lay the saying up as a deposit — and the pronoun distinguishes them, since the multitude were not to know he was about to suffer but were to be assured instead that the dead would rise.

What the sayings are is disputed. Gill takes them to be not the words already spoken but the prediction about to follow, and Clarke and Wesley read the charge as a rule of attention — other words may be given occasional hearing, but what concerns his sufferings must always be listened to, and in joy one must remember the cross, our Lord wisely balancing praise with suffering. Barnes offers two readings and prefers the one the Greek supports less well, that the sayings are the people's, who had glorified God at the miracle and so acknowledged him: remember this evidence, he paraphrases, when I am dead and you are disconsolate and doubtful whether I was the Christ. His alternative, which he grants fits the Greek better, is simply that the coming death is the thing to be lodged in memory against the day it happens. Robertson corrects the English rendering, since there is no word answering to sink: the verb means put, and the emphatic pronoun makes it do you yourselves, whatever others may do, put these words into your ears.

On the failure to understand, Robertson notes that the concealment is reported by Luke alone, in a verb found nowhere else in the New Testament, and that the clause of purpose at least relieves the disciples of full responsibility for their ignorance. Gill locates the obstacle precisely: they could not reconcile a betrayal and a death with the notions they held of a temporal redeemer and a victorious Messiah. Barnes turns that into the lesson he wants, that the hiding was not God's doing but their own previous false belief, and generalises it without hedging — the plainest truths of the Bible are unintelligible to many because they have already embraced an erroneous opinion they are unwilling to abandon, so that the proper way to read is to lay aside all previous opinions and submit entirely. The apostles, he says, should have supposed their notion of the Messiah wrong rather than the words of Jesus, and should have believed that what he said was consistent with his being the Christ.
46:
Cyril treats the dispute as a case of tactics: the devil lays plots of various kinds against those who love the best way of life, sharpening the love of pleasure where he can take a heart by carnal allurement, and where a man has escaped that snare exciting in him a desire of glory instead — which is what had seized one of the apostles. He then reads the wording as a kindness. To think such thoughts belongs to a man who wants to be above the rest, and Cyril judges it improbable that all the disciples gave way; so he takes the Evangelist's indefinite phrase, that there arose a reasoning among them, as deliberately framed to avoid laying the charge against any individual. Gill notices where the reasoning happened and how it was known: the dispute was on the road, behind Christ and out of his hearing, and he perceived it not by any word he had heard but as the omniscient God who is the discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.

Robertson reconstructs the scene from the three accounts together, the disciples in a circle, the child taken to himself and then set down at his side rather than in his arms or in the midst as the others have it, and wonders in passing whether it was Peter's child; the point, he says, was an object lesson in humility which they sorely needed. Ellicott corrects the verb, which is rather laid hold on than took. Gill guards the child from sentimentality, insisting that likeness to it is not in age but in meekness and humility, in not being proud or ambitious of worldly honour or envious of another's better place. Ellicott then finds the sharpest thing in the pericope in a variant: the better manuscripts do not read that the least shall be great but that he is great, so that the greatness is not deferred as a compensation in some far-off future but attained now, in the midst of the seeming humiliation and by means of it. The clause itself, in this place and this form, he notes is peculiar to Luke.

Robertson reads John's interruption psychologically, as an attempt to change the subject after the embarrassment of the rebuke, and does not spare him: it is a pitiful specimen of partisan narrowness and pride even in the Beloved Disciple, one of the sons of thunder, since the man was doing the Master's work in the Master's name and with the Master's power and merely did not run with the group of the Twelve. He notes that the verb is a conative imperfect, so they tried to hinder rather than succeeded, and that the prohibition in reply is likewise a present imperative, stop hindering him. Ambrose is gentler with John, allowing that he loved much and was much beloved, and only thought that those who did not practise obedience should be shut out from the privilege. Theophylact draws the conclusion the incident invites, that we should marvel at the power of Christ, whose grace works through the unworthy and through those who are not his disciples, as men are sanctified through priests who are not themselves holy. Robertson adds that the saying is proverbial and that the lesson of toleration in methods of work for Christ is needed still.
51:
The verse turns on what the receiving up means, and the room divides. Barnes and Robertson take it of the ascension: the word denotes a removal from a lower place to a higher and is used elsewhere of that event, and Robertson adds that it stands here alone in the New Testament, is old enough to be found in Hippocrates, and shows that Jesus was fully conscious how near his death was. Barnes draws the conclusion he wants from it — that the sacrifice was voluntary, since humanly speaking he would have been safe had he stayed in Galilee, and he put himself in the way of danger to show that no man had power over his life. Clarke reports Bishop Pearce against this, on a grammatical ground: the verb before it denotes a time completed, which the ascension then was not, so the word must mean his withdrawing, and the sense is that the time was past for retiring from Judea as he had hitherto done, having lived in Galilee lest the Jews should lay hold on him before his ministry was finished. Calvin keeps both, calling the death an ἀνάληψις not only because he was then withdrawn from the midst of us but because, leaving the mean prison of the flesh, he ascended on high.

Calvin also says why the passage is worth having, since Luke alone relates it: it shows the divine courage and firmness of Christ in despising death, what deadly enmities are produced by differences about religion, how headlong human nature is towards impatience, how ready we are to go wrong in imitating the saints, and how we are called by his example to meekness. Robertson notes the emphatic pronoun in the setting of the face and calls the idiom Hebraistic, found nine times in Ezekiel, while the verb itself means to fix or make fast; the same look is remarked later by Mark as Jesus went to his doom. Cyril states the occasion plainly, that the time being near in which he must accomplish his life-giving passion and ascend, he determined to go up. Lightfoot answers an objection to the wording — why speak of a receiving up where there is no mention of death — by taking the decease to be included in it, and then makes the phrase a chronological frame: from this point Christ resolved to be present at all the feasts preceding it, going first to Tabernacles, ten weeks later to the Dedication, and at length to his own Passover.

On the messengers Barnes and Clarke both notice that the word is literally angels, and both draw the same lexical conclusion, that the term does not always mean heavenly beings; Gill and Clarke guess the two were James and John, which would explain their resentment afterwards. Barnes adds a domestic moral, that since Christ made provision beforehand it is not improper to look ahead and guard against want. Lightfoot asks whether Jews would ordinarily lodge in a Samaritan town at all and answers that nothing but hatred forbade it, since their land and waters and dwellings and roads were reckoned clean, and their religion came nearer the Jewish than any other. Ellicott observes that Samaria and Samaritan do not occur in Mark at all and in Matthew only once, and that Luke by contrast seems to have carried his inquiries into the country and treasured whatever he could find of Christ's words about it. Barnes explains the refusal by the old dispute over where the temple belonged, Gerizim against Jerusalem, and supposes they had hoped Jesus would decide for them; when they saw him going to Jerusalem instead they rejected him — from which he concludes that men wish all teachers of religion to fall in with their own views, and reject without examination whatever favours a rival.
54:
Everyone notices that these are the sons of thunder, and most think the place itself put the thought into their heads. Barnes takes the name to have been given either for energy in preaching or for vehement and rash zeal, and says this is a remarkable instance of the latter; Ellicott finds their fire more than Peter's and thinks their anger was sharpened by the contrast with the welcome Christ had once had in another city of the same people, so that what seemed to them a marvellous condescension had been rudely repelled. Wesley notes that Elisha did the like at or near this very spot, which is why the motion was made here rather than after some other affront, and Calvin says the same of the country having suggested the desire to thunder. Robertson adds that the recent appearance of Elijah on the mountain may have brought the old incident to mind, and that the two disciples quote the Greek of Kings when they ask. Clarke answers them in a sentence: vengeance belongs to the Lord, and what we suffer for his sake should be left to him to reprove or punish, the insult being offered to him and not to us.

Calvin makes the episode a case study in bad imitation, and it is the fullest treatment in the pericope. Here, he says, we see what a foolish copying of the holy fathers drives us to: men plead the example of Elijah without considering how far they differ from him, without examining their own intemperate zeal, and without looking at the calling of God — and the Samaritans had cloaked their own idolatry under a pretext just as plausible, so that both parties, neglecting judgement, were apes rather than imitators. His rule from the reply is correspondingly general. Whoever undertakes anything ought to be sure he has the authority and guidance of the Spirit, since many are impelled by the warmth of their zeal but, wanting prudence, their ebullitions end in foam; and it often happens that the impure feelings of the flesh mingle with zeal, so that those who seem keenest for God's glory are blinded by private feeling. Elijah executed a judgement committed to him; these two rushed at vengeance by the movement of the flesh. The examples of the saints, he concludes, are no defence to us unless the same Spirit that directed them dwells in us.

Ellicott sets out two ways of construing the rebuke — that the disciples did not know the Spirit given to their Master and promised to them was one of gentleness, or that in yielding to what they took for righteous anger they were yielding to the evil mind at enmity with God — and prefers the first as agreeing better with what follows, since the Spirit that had claimed them led him to save and not to destroy. Lightfoot suspects them of hearing thunder and lightning in their own new name and supposing it might break out at pleasure. But the textual question shadows the whole passage, and three voices raise it independently. Ellicott notes that the clause about the spirit is wanting in the best manuscripts and that the following sentence is absent from many good ones too, conjecturing that it may have come in from an oral tradition; Clarke lists the manuscripts, reports that Griesbach removes the latter clause from the text, and reconstructs what the most ancient copies probably read — he turned and rebuked them, and they went to another village. Barnes, untroubled, takes the disputed words as the point of the story and turns them into a charge: imitate the Son of man in your spirit, temper your zeal like his, and seek to do good to those who injure you.
57:
Cyril hears presumption in the first offer. God is bountiful but does not give heavenly gifts indiscriminately, only to those who free their souls from the stains of wickedness; and this man's approach shows both tardiness in the coming and too great confidence in the asking, since he sought not simply to follow as others of the people did but caught at the honour of the apostleship — whereas, Cyril quotes, no man takes that honour to himself but he that is called of God. Gill raises the question of where the incident belongs, noting that the words on both sides are exactly those in Matthew, which makes it look like the same history, though he allows that Christ might have been accosted the same way twice and answered alike; and on the setting he observes that if it is Matthew's account it stood in a different journey altogether and has been inserted here without regard to the order of time. Wesley reduces the answer about the foxes to a single instruction: first understand the terms, and consider on what conditions you are to follow.

The second man's request divides the commentators on a point of fact. Robertson supposes the father was probably still alive, as in the similar case in Tobit, so that what the scribe meant was that he could not leave a living father to follow Jesus about the country; and he sets the problem in its general form, that one of the difficulties of life is the relation of duties to each other and which of them comes first, burial being a sacred duty of long standing. He also notes that Matthew omits the call to follow and so makes the man a volunteer, and passes on Plummer's description of him as one of the casual disciples of whom there are always too many, adding that the scribes knew how to give plausible reasons for not being active ones. Chrysostom takes the possessive in the reply as decisive in the other direction: by saying their dead Christ shows that this man's father was not his dead, the deceased having been, he supposes, of the number of the unbelieving.

Lightfoot supplies the idiom behind the paradox from Jewish usage, where the Gentiles were reckoned simply as dead — the people of the earth do not live — and where four sorts were accounted dead even among themselves, the blind, the leprous, the poor and the childless. Robertson states the paradox plainly, that the spiritually dead can bury the literally dead. Ambrose faces the difficulty squarely rather than explaining it away: burial is a religious duty we have received, so how can the burial even of a father's body be forbidden, unless human things are to be postponed to divine? His answer is about attention rather than affection — the employment is good, but the hindrance is greater, for a man who divides his pursuits draws down his affections and a man who divides his care delays his progress, so that what is most important must be set about first; and he finds the apostles doing the same thing when they ordained others to distribute alms rather than be occupied in it themselves. Bede turns the severity forward on the reader: if a disciple is reproved for wishing merely to take leave at home, what shall be said of those who for no advantage keep visiting the houses of the people they left behind in the world?
61:
Gill and Calvin both note that this third man is Luke's alone, Matthew having only two, and Calvin reads him as one too strongly attached to the world to be ready: he offers to join the family of Christ, but with a reservation, as men do when preparing for a journey, and that is why the reproof is so severe, since he professed in words to be a follower while turning his back until his worldly business was despatched. Ellicott finds the same hollowness by a different route. The offer looks spontaneous and is coupled at once with a plea for delay; and since no father or wife or children is named, he half suspects the man was free of the closer and more binding ties altogether, so that the plea was unreal. Robertson is more careful with him, observing that the pronoun means simply another rather than one of a different sort, and that taking leave of one's household was in itself a good thing to do — the trouble being only that he too had something which had to come first. He adds that the verb is an old military one, to detach or to assign as a detachment of soldiers.

Clarke prefers a different rendering and thinks the Greek supports it better: permit me to set my affairs in order at home. On that reading the man had Elisha's case in view, whose identical request Elijah granted; and Clarke explains the refusal by the difference in the men, since Christ saw too much attachment to earth here, and saw that even a short return to worldly employment was likely to stifle the desires the man now felt. He states the principle as an aphorism — that what we plead against the execution of God's designs is sometimes the very thing we ought to disengage from immediately. Barnes reaches the same refusal by supposing the man would have been worked on by his friends and persuaded not to come back, and turns it into a rule about counsel: the purpose to be a Christian requires decision, and a man should not tamper with the world, nor consult earthly friends about it, nor even let worldly friends advise him whether to be a Christian at all, God being to be obeyed rather than man.

On the ploughman both commentators take the figure literally enough to work it. Barnes calls putting the hand to the plough a proverb for undertaking any business, and says the ploughman must look onward and be intent on his employment rather than looking back with regret that he began; so in religion, since a man who still loves the world and looks with regret at its pleasures and honours has not forsaken them as his portion. His conclusion is the flattest in the chapter: religion is everything or nothing, and he who is not willing to sacrifice everything for the cause of God is really willing to sacrifice nothing. Clarke keeps the furrow and adds the trade detail, that a man holding the plough cannot keep it straight if he looks behind him, then applies it narrowly to the ministry and asks whether anyone engaged in secular employment can properly discharge that work, calling a farmer and a minister of the gospel incompatible characters. He quotes a saying to the same effect, that whoever thinks it necessary to cultivate the favour of the world is not far from betraying the interests of God and his church, and glosses the word for fitness as properly disposed, so that such a man is not fit to show others the way. Both note that these two verses look back to the call of Elisha.
